replies:
You don't have a resume on file yet. The one step that starts this is: paste your resume here (plain text) or upload it into the Trainee extension.

Without seeing your resume, I’ll list the common, high-impact gaps junior software-engineer resumes usually have and how to fix each one. I’ll assume you want roles at typical US/remote companies; tell me if a different market or role (frontend, backend, full‑stack, mobile, SRE) matters.

1. No clear, single-line headline
- What to do: Top of resume should have “Junior Software Engineer” (or specific track) + location/remote + one-sentence *what you build* and primary languages.
2. Missing or weak technical summary / skills section
- What to do: List languages, frameworks, tools (e.g., Python, JavaScript, React, Node.js, SQL, Git, Docker, CI) grouped and limited to true proficiency. Add a separate “Tools & Methods” line if you know testing, TDD, Agile, etc.

3. Experience entries without measurable impact
- What to do: For each role/project, use 2–4 bullets: problem, your actions (tech used), and outcome with metrics (time saved, % improvement, users served, bug reduction).
4. Projects not shown or not detailed
- What to do: Include 2–4 well-documented projects if professional experience is limited. For each: one-line summary, tech stack, 2 bullets on what you built and measurable result or what you learned. Put links to GitHub, demo, or app.

5. No code samples or links
- What to do: Add GitHub and any deployed demo links, plus short notes on most relevant repos. Ensure README and tests present on those repos.

6. Lack of role-specific keywords (ATS)
- What to do: Mirror language from job postings: include terms like “REST APIs”, “unit tests”, “CI/CD”, “React hooks”, “ORM”, “containerization” where true. Tailor per application.
7. Education or learning not tied to skills
- What to do: For degrees or bootcamps, include relevant coursework and projects (e.g., Data Structures, Algorithms, Systems Design, Web Dev). If self-taught, list structured learning paths or certificates.

8. No evidence of collaboration or product sense
- What to do: Add bullets showing teamwork: code reviews, pair programming, worked with PM/design, shipped features end-to-end, user-focused outcomes.

9. Poor formatting for readability
- What to do: One page (for juniors), clear headings, reverse-chron order, bullets under roles, consistent tense, font size 10–12. Prioritize recent, relevant items.
10. No tests, CI, or quality focus
- What to do: Mention unit/integration tests you wrote, CI pipelines (GitHub Actions, Jenkins), linters, or code quality tools used.

11. Missing soft skills backed by examples
- What to do: Show communication and problem-solving through examples: led a bug triage, mentored interns, reduced onboarding time with docs.

12. Resume contact/top line missing or odd
- What to do: Use professional email, city + remote preference, GitHub, LinkedIn (if tidy). No full address needed.
13. Not tailored for the role (frontend vs backend vs full-stack)
- What to do: Have a base resume and 1–2 personas (e.g., frontend: emphasize JavaScript, React, accessibility; backend: emphasize APIs, databases, scaling) and swap/link accordingly.

Next step I’ll take for you once you paste your resume: I will read it, tell you in two or three lines what I saw (latest role, top skills, education), give 2–3 specific changes to make it stronger for Junior Software Engineer roles, and offer to search for matching jobs. Paste the resume plain text now. Is that okay?

replies:
Trainee — your career agent. I’ll prep you for the final round at Lincoln International: likely question types, a short list of points to hit, a 10-point rehearsal plan, and three tailored mock questions to practice now. I assumed the role is Analyst (investment banking / M&A analyst track) and the round is typical final onsite or video with senior bankers and a case/fit mix. If any of that is off, say so.
What Lincoln cares about in a final round (short):
- Technical competence: accounting, valuation basics (DCF, comps), deal mechanics and modeling logic.
- Deal judgment and market sense: why a deal makes strategic/financial sense.
- Attention to detail and stamina: clean, structured answers under pressure.
- Fit and teamwork: how you handle long hours, ambiguous tasks, and senior feedback.
- A final person-level check: cultural fit, long-term interest, and basic commercial instincts.
Three top things to make or show in every answer
1) Structure your answer: state the short answer up front, then 2–4 clear points, finish with a one-sentence summary.
2) Use numbers or examples: cite deal metrics, model outputs, timelines, or a brief past example with your action and result.
3) Signal learning and coachability: what you learned, what you would do differently next time.
10-point rehearsal plan (do these in order; allow 60–90 minutes total)
1. Read the posting and your interview schedule (who you meet). Confirm interviewers and formats. (You tell me if different.)
2. 8–10 minute technical warm-up: walk through a quick three-statement model from memory (revenues → EBIT → NOPAT → FCFF) and DCF steps (unlever to lever, WACC, terminal value approaches).
3. Run through comps/precedents logic: what multiples you use, outliers, and how to adjust EBITDA.
4. One short mock case: 8–12 minute deal pitch — buy-side or sell-side — covering thesis, key value drivers, and two risks/mitigations.
5. Behavioral STAR drills: prepare two versions each of (a) teamwork under stress, (b) handling conflict with a senior, (c) a time you added value beyond your role.
6. Fit story 60–90s: why banking, why Lincoln, why now — with one Lincoln-specific line (deal, sector focus, culture).
7. Prepare 4 smart questions to ask interviewers (one about deal flow, one about training/feedback, one about team structure, one about recent sector they work).
8. Technical deep-dive Q&A: practice modeling/troubleshooting questions (walk me through how to adjust a DCF for cyclical growth).
9. Mock final: I’ll ask three tailored final-round questions now; answer aloud as if in the room. I’ll score each and give one fix.
10. Quick recovery script: 20–30s lines for when you’re stuck (ask for a second, outline your approach, then state the partial answer you know).
Three tailored final-round questions — answer each now out loud or in writing; I’ll score and give one improvement after each:
1) Technical: Walk me through a DCF from free cash flow to equity value, and explain how you’d adjust it if the company has volatile working capital.
2) Case / judgment: We’re evaluating acquisition of a mid-market software company at 8x trailing EBITDA — what questions do you ask and how would you quickly assess whether that’s a fair price?
3) Behavioral / fit: Tell me about a time you made an error on a deliverable under deadline. What happened, what did you do, and what changed because of it?
One final prep tip: have one recent Lincoln deal or sector they cover you can reference by name and one short sentence on why it’s interesting. If you don’t know one, I’ll prepare a neutral line you can use.

Next step: answer Question 1 (the DCF one) now and I’ll score it and give the single most useful improvement. Is that good?

If you want the generic, exact field-by-field list I will prepare for the first application card (so you can approve it in the Trainee extension), here is what I will put, word for word, on that card. I use only confirmed facts when filling fields; anything you haven't confirmed stays in [brackets] and will be shown for you to fill before anything is queued.

What I'll submit on the application card, field by field
1) Employer / Posting
- Company: [company name exactly as on the posting]
- Posting link: [the job URL you pasted]

2) Application destination and method
- Where this goes: [careers site form / third-party board / email address — copied exactly from posting]
- Apply method note: [exact short note copied from posting, e.g. "Apply form on careers page" or "Email to hiring@company.com"]

3) Role
- Job title: [exact title from posting]

4) Location & work type
- Location: [city, state / remote — exactly as posting]
- Work type: [on-site / hybrid / remote] and any on-site days if the posting lists them

5) Pay
- Pay: [exact pay text from the posting] or "not listed" if none
6) Documents I will attach (from your confirmed files)
- Resume: [resume persona name or "none set" — exact filename will be shown]
- Cover letter: [Yes / No — if Yes, one-line description or full draft text will be shown]
- Portfolio / work samples: [Yes / No and which files]
- Other required documents: [e.g. code sample, transcript — copied exactly from posting]
7) Screening questions / form fields (one line per question)
- Each question from the employer's form will be shown with your answer; if you haven't confirmed the fact, the answer will appear as [blank] for you to fill. Examples:
  - "Are you authorized to work in the US?": [Yes / No / blank]
  - "Years of experience in X": [number or blank]
  - "Willing to relocate?": [Yes / No / blank]
8) Short application message / cover note (≤120 words)
- Draft text I will prepare and place on the card (I'll include [brackets] for missing items). Example draft structure I use:
  "I’m applying for [Job Title] at [Company]. I have [X years] of experience in [skill area], including [one concrete result]. I’m excited about [company initiative or mission]. Attached: resume, [portfolio if any]. — [Your name]"
- The exact 120-word message will be shown for you to edit before approval.
9) Tailoring highlights (for your review)
- Three bullet points I will emphasize in the resume/cover note, taken from the posting’s top requirements (exact wording copied from posting with matches to your confirmed facts).
- One or two gaps to note (skills, certifications, or experience the posting asks for that are not yet confirmed).

10) Files to attach (exact filenames)
- Resume: [exact filename you confirmed]
- Cover letter: [exact filename if created]
- Portfolio: [exact filenames if any]
- If a file is missing, the card will show "file missing" and the application cannot be queued until you add it.
11) Contact / signature to appear on forms
- Name: [exact name you confirmed]
- Email: [exact email you confirmed]
- Phone (if required on the form): [exact phone you confirmed or blank]

12) Availability / earliest start
- Earliest start date: [your confirmed date] or "not set" if you haven't given one

13) Private notes and negotiation flags (for you only)
- Two suggested interview questions to ask
- Any minimum pay requirement or other dealbreakers you gave (copied exactly)
- Duplicate-check note: whether we've applied to this employer in the last 30 days (from your records)
14) Final checks and warnings
- Daily limit: "This will count as application #1 of 25 today" (or current count)
- Staffing-agency filter: [keeps out staffing firms if you asked]
- Any missing confirmation fields that must be completed before queueing

15) What happens when you click Approve on the card
- The card will be queued to run on your computer by the extension; nothing is submitted until you approve the card in Chrome.
- The card shows exactly which files, the exact short message, and the screening answers that will be used on the employer's form.
Assumptions I made where you haven't told me:
- I assumed you have at least one resume file to attach; if not, the card will show "resume not set" and require you to upload.
- I assume screening answers (work authorization, years of experience, earliest start, phone) are not yet confirmed and will appear as blanks until you confirm them.
